newsitem.title: USA: US jobs created by new firms up 15 pct in 96-study.
newsitem.headline: US jobs created by new firms up 15 pct in 96-study.

text.p: Throughout the U.S. economy, newly-started businesses made a siginificantly greater contribution to employment growth in 1996 than in the previous year, according to a Dun & Bradstreet Corp study released on Monday.
The number of new businesses started in 1996 rose to 170,475, a gain of about 1.0 percent from 1995, the study showed.
Those businesses, however, created a total of 846,973 new jobs, an increase of 15 percent from jobs created by new businesses in 1995, the study said.

"The U.S. economy supported very healthy levels of entreprenurial activity in 1996, and those small, start-up businesses were a major factor in the strong employment growth we saw during the year," said Joseph Duncan, chief economic advisor to Dun & Bradstreet.
"The strong level of job creation means that last year's new business activity will have a lasting impact on the U.S. economy," Duncan added.
Nearly every key industry sector saw higher levels of business and job creation during 1996, the study said.
The services sector was among the strongest performers, with a 12 percent rise in new business starts and a 19-percent gain in job creation, according to the Dun & Bradstreet study.
The construction industry also grew faster in 1996, with 10 percent more new business starts and 21 percent more jobs created by new businesses, it said.
The transportation and public utilities sector saw a 12 percent increase in new businesses and a 15 percent increase in job creation, based on the study.
"Many new businesses benefitted from a surge in capital investment activity that took place during 1996," Duncan said.

"Industrial contractors and builders, utilities, and producers of industrial equipment and raw materials were among the most active sectors for entrepreneurial activity," said the chief economic advisor to Dun & Bradstreet.
"However, last year's new business activity also reflects high levels of consumer confidence," Duncan said.
"Together, the retail and services sectors accounted for more than 478,000 new jobs, over half of all employment growth associated with new business starts in 1996," he added.
The finance, insurance and real estate sector experienced an 8.0 percent increase in new business starts, and a 12.0 percent rise in job creation, the study showed.
Business starts rose by 7.0 percent in the wholesale trade sector, and job creation increased by 15.0 percent, based on the Dun & Bradstreet study.
Most other sectors experienced growth of about 4.0 to 6.0 percent in the number of new business starts, but several showed significantly faster growth in job creation, it said.
New retail establishments hired 200,354 employees during 1996, 14 percent more than in 1995, the study said.
Employment associated with new businesses jumped 27.0 percent in the agriculture, forestry and fishing sector, and 48.0 percent in the mining sector, it said.

The study said nonclassifiable businesses were the only industry category to show lower numbers of business starts and new employment. This group, however, is often characterized by incomplete information and is not reliably comparable.

Consistent with the overall results for the U.S. economy, most regions of the country reported steady numbers of new business starts and higher levels of employment associated with those businesses, the Dun & Bradstreet study said.
The strongest growth took place in the Mountain region, where new business starts rose 10.0 percent compared with 1995 and associated employment was up by 32 percent, it said.

The East South Central and West South Central regions both saw a 5.0 percent rise in new business starts and increased job creation of 4.0 and 16.0 percent, respectively, based on the Dun & Bradstreet study.
New business starts were essentially flat at 31,100 in the Middle Atlantic states, however associated job creation increased by 19.0 percent, the study showed.
In New England, 8,960 new businesses were started in 1996, down three percent from the previous year. Yet those businesses created about 45,900 new jobs, an increase of 18 percent from 1995, it said.
The Pacific region experienced only a small gain in the number of new businesses, but saw a 24 percent rise in new job creation, according to the Dun & Bradstreet study.

The East North Central, West North Central and South Atlantic regions all reported approximately even levels of new business starts and increases of 5.0 to 9.0 percent in associated job creation, the study showed.
((-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660))
